title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 27
paragraphs: At the appointed hour, the prince—powdered and freshly shaved—entered the dining room, where his daughter-in-law, Princess Mary, and Mademoiselle Bourienne were already waiting, along with his architect. By one of the old prince's strange whims, this architect was admitted to the dinner table, even though his rank was far too modest to warrant such an honor. The prince, who was generally strict about social distinctions and seldom invited even important government officials to dine, had unexpectedly chosen Mikhail Ivanovich—a man who always retreated to a corner to blow his nose into a checkered handkerchief—to illustrate his theory that all men are equal. He had impressed upon his daughter more than once that Mikhail Ivanovich was "not one bit worse than you or me." At dinner, the prince usually directed more of his conversation at the silent Mikhail Ivanovich than at anyone else.

In the dining room—which, like every room in the house, had extraordinarily high ceilings—the household members and the footmen (one stationed behind each chair) stood waiting for the prince to appear. The head butler, napkin draped over his arm, was inspecting the table settings, signaling to the footmen, and glancing nervously between the clock and the door through which the prince would enter. Prince Andrei was studying a large gilt frame, new to him, that held the Bolkonsky family tree. Opposite it hung a matching frame with a poorly painted portrait—clearly the work of a local artist—of a prince in a crown, supposedly a descendant of Rurik and ancestor of the Bolkonskys. Prince Andrei looked again at the family tree, shook his head, and laughed the way one laughs at a portrait so perfectly capturing its subject that it becomes comical.
"That's so completely him!" he said to Princess Mary, who had come up beside him.
Princess Mary looked at her brother in surprise. She didn't understand what he found funny. Everything their father did filled her with reverence and was beyond questioning.
"Everyone has their weak spot," Prince Andrei continued. "Imagine—with his formidable intellect, indulging in this kind of vanity!"

Princess Mary couldn't fathom the audacity of her brother's criticism and was about to respond when the expected footsteps were heard coming from the study. The prince walked in briskly and jauntily, as was his way, as though deliberately setting the liveliness of his manner against the rigid formality of his household. At that instant, the great clock struck two and was joined by a smaller clock chiming from the drawing room. The prince stopped. His sharp, glittering eyes swept sternly over everyone present and came to rest on the little princess. She felt what courtiers feel when the Tsar enters—a rush of fear and deference that the old man inspired in everyone around him. He stroked her hair and then gave her an awkward pat on the back of her neck.
"I'm glad—glad to see you," he said, looking attentively into her eyes, then walked quickly to his place and sat down. "Sit down, sit down! Sit down, Mikhail Ivanovich!"
He indicated a seat beside him for his daughter-in-law. A footman pulled out the chair for her.
"Well, well!" the old man said, eyeing her rounded figure. "You've been in quite a hurry. Not good!"
He laughed in his usual dry, cold, unpleasant way—with his lips only, not his eyes.
"You need to walk—walk as much as possible, as much as possible," he said.

The little princess either didn't hear his words or chose not to. She sat silent and seemed ill at ease. The prince asked about her father, and she began to smile and talk. He asked about mutual acquaintances, and she grew more animated, chattering away, passing on greetings from various people and retelling the latest society gossip.
"Countess Apraksina, the poor thing, lost her husband—she's cried her eyes out," she said, growing more and more lively.

As she became more animated, the prince studied her with increasing severity, and then suddenly, as if he had observed her long enough and formed a definite opinion, he turned away and addressed Mikhail Ivanovich.

"Well, Mikhail Ivanovich, things aren't looking good for our friend Bonaparte. Prince Andrei"—he always referred to his son this way—"has been telling me what forces are being gathered against him! And you and I never did think much of him."

Mikhail Ivanovich had no idea when "you and I" had ever said any such thing about Bonaparte, but understanding that he was being used as a convenient prop for the prince's favorite subject, he looked inquiringly at the young prince, wondering what would come next.
"He's a great tactician!" the prince said to his son, nodding toward the architect.

The conversation turned again to the war, to Bonaparte, and to the generals and statesmen of the day. The old prince seemed convinced not only that every man of the current age was an infant who didn't know the ABCs of warfare or politics, and that Bonaparte was an insignificant little Frenchman who had succeeded only because there were no Potemkins or Suvorovs left to oppose him—but also that there were no real political difficulties in Europe and no real war, only a sort of puppet show in which the men of the day were playing at something serious. Prince Andrei cheerfully endured his father's mockery of modern leaders, drawing him out and listening with obvious enjoyment.
"The past always seems better," he said. "But didn't Suvorov himself walk into a trap set by Moreau, from which he couldn't escape?"

"Who told you that? Who?" the prince cried. "Suvorov!" He shoved his plate away—Tikhon caught it deftly. "Suvorov!... Think, Prince Andrei. Two great commanders—Frederick and Suvorov. Moreau!... Moreau would have been taken prisoner if Suvorov had been given a free hand. But he had the Austrian war council—the Hofskriegsratschnapswurst—on his back. The devil himself couldn't have managed them! When you get out there, you'll see what those councils are really like! Suvorov couldn't handle them—so what chance does Mikhail Kutuzov have? No, my boy," he continued, "you and your generals won't be a match for Bonaparte. You'll have to bring in the French so that birds of a feather can fight together. They've sent the German Pahlen to New York to fetch the Frenchman Moreau," he said, referring to the invitation extended that year for Moreau to enter Russian service. "Wonderful!... Were the Potemkins, Suvorovs, and Orlovs Germans? No, my boy—either you've all lost your minds, or I've outlived mine. God help you, and we'll see what happens. They've made Bonaparte into a great commander among them! Ha!..."
"I'm not saying all the plans are good," Prince Andrei said. "I'm just surprised by your opinion of Bonaparte. Laugh all you want, but Bonaparte is a great general all the same!"

"Mikhail Ivanovich!" the old prince called to the architect, who had been quietly focused on his roast and was hoping to be forgotten. "Didn't I tell you Bonaparte was a great tactician? And now he's saying the same thing."
"Absolutely, your excellency," the architect replied.
The prince let out another of his cold laughs.

"Bonaparte was born lucky. He's got excellent soldiers. And besides, he started out by fighting Germans. Anyone who isn't a complete fool has been able to beat the Germans. Since the beginning of history, everyone has beaten the Germans. They've never beaten anyone—except each other. He made his reputation fighting them."

And the prince launched into a detailed account of all the blunders that, in his view, Bonaparte had made in his campaigns and even in politics. His son offered no rebuttal, but it was clear that no argument would change his mind any more than it would change his father's. He listened, held back his responses, and couldn't help marveling at how this old man, living alone in the country for so many years, could be so well-informed and so incisive about every recent military and political development in Europe.

"You think I'm just an old man who doesn't understand the world today?" his father concluded. "But it keeps me up at night. Well, tell me—where has this great commander of yours actually shown his genius?"
"That would take too long to explain," the son replied.
"Fine then, go worship your Bonaparte! Mademoiselle Bourienne, here's another admirer of that gunpowder-monkey emperor of yours," he said in excellent French.
"You know, Prince, I am not a Bonapartist!"
"[Speaking in French] God knows when he'll return," the prince hummed, out of tune, and with a laugh even more so, he left the table.

Throughout the entire discussion and the rest of dinner, the little princess had sat in silence, her frightened eyes darting between her father-in-law and Princess Mary. When they rose from the table, she took her sister-in-law by the arm and pulled her into another room.
"What a brilliant man your father is," she said. "Perhaps that's why I'm afraid of him."
"Oh, he is so kind!" Princess Mary answered.
